sections.title: Basic agreement rules
sections.content:
If a sentence has a singular subject, it is followed by a singular verb, and if it has a plural subject, it is followed by a plural verb; that is, the verb agrees with the subject. Compare:
• She lives in China. and • More people live in Asia than in any other continent.
When the subject of the sentence is complex, the following verb must agree with the main noun in the subject:
• Many leading members of the opposition party have criticised the delay.
• The only excuse that he gave for his actions was that he was tired.
The verb must agree with the subject when the subject follows the verb:
• Displayed on the board were the exam results. (compare The exam results were displayed ...)

sections.title: Clauses as subjects
sections.content:
If the subject is a clause, we usually use a singular verb:
• To keep these young people in prison is inhuman.
• Having overall responsibility for the course means that I have a lot of meetings.
• Whoever took them remains a mystery.
However, if we use a what-clause as subject, we use a singular verb if the following main noun is singular, and either a singular or a plural verb if the following main noun is plural (although a plural verb is preferred in more formal contexts):
• What worries us is the poor selection process.
• What is needed are additional resources. (or more colloquially ... needed is ...)

sections.title: Collective nouns (groups)
sections.content:
Some nouns with a singular form, referring to groups of some kind, can be used with either a singular or plural form of the verb. These nouns are sometimes called collective nouns:
• The council has (or have) postponed a decision on the new road.
We use a singular verb if the institution or organisation is thought of as a whole unit, and a plural verb if it is thought of as a collection of individuals. Often you can use either with very little difference in meaning, although in formal contexts (such as academic writing) it is common to use a singular verb.
Also: army, association, audience, class, club, college, commission, committee, community, company, crew, crowd, department, electorate, enemy, family, federation, generation, government, group, institute, jury, opposition, orchestra, population, press, public, school, team, university; the Bank of England, the BBC, IBM, Sony, the United Nations
In some contexts we have to use a singular or a plural form of the verb:
• The committee usually raise their hands to vote 'Yes'. (This is something the individuals do, not the committee as a whole.)
• The school is to close next year. (This is something that will happen to the school as a building or institution, not to the individuals in the school.)

sections.title: Names and titles ending in -s
sections.content:
When names and titles ending in -s refer to a single unit we use a singular verb. Examples include countries; newspapers; titles of books, films, etc.; and quoted plural words or phrases:
• At this time of the year the Netherlands is one hour ahead of the UK.
• The Machine Gunners was one of Robert Westall's most successful books.
• 'Daps' is the word used in the south-west of the country for sports shoes.

exercises.question: The museum's incredible collection of seashells and fossils in the final room ___ sure to be of interest.
exercises.hint: The main noun in the subject block is 'collection' (singular).
exercises.explanation:
Answer: is
The main noun in the subject block is 'collection' (singular).

exercises.sentence: Neither the manager nor the employees was informed about the changes.
exercises.correction: Neither the manager nor the employees were informed about the changes.
exercises.hint: With 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the nearest subject ('employees' = plural).
exercises.explanation:
Answer: the employees were informed
With 'neither...nor' and 'either...or', the verb agrees with the subject NEAREST to it (proximity rule). Here, 'employees' (plural) is nearest to the verb, so use 'were'. If 'manager' were nearest: 'Neither the employees nor the manager was informed'.

exercises.question: Whoever created these figures apparently ___ a mystery.
exercises.hint: A clause as subject ('Whoever created these figures') takes a singular verb.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: remains
A clause as subject ('Whoever created these figures') takes a singular verb.

exercises.sentence: The news are very worrying — have you seen the latest reports?
exercises.correction: The news is very worrying — have you seen the latest reports?
exercises.hint: 'News' is an uncountable noun — always singular, even though it ends in -s.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: The news is very worrying
'News' is uncountable in English despite the -s ending and always takes a singular verb. Other similar nouns: 'economics is', 'mathematics is', 'physics is', 'the United States is', 'measles is'. These are grammatically singular even though they look plural.

exercises.question: The junior book prize jury ___ three adults and three children. (Select one choice that cannot be wrong in either British or American style depending on context, or focus on the fact that they consist of individuals but form a single entity).
exercises.hint: Collective nouns like 'jury' can take singular or plural verbs.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: both 'include' and 'includes'
Collective nouns like 'jury' can take singular or plural verbs.

exercises.sentence: A large number of students has complained about the new policy.
exercises.correction: A large number of students have complained about the new policy.
acceptable: A large number of students have complained
exercises.hint: 'A number of' = several/many → plural verb. 'The number of' = a specific count → singular verb.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: A large number of students have complained
'A number of + plural noun' takes a plural verb because the meaning is 'several/many'. Contrast with 'THE number of + plural noun', which takes a singular verb: 'The number of complaints has increased'. This distinction is consistently tested at advanced level.

exercises.question: The phrase 'men in white coats' ___ used to talk about psychiatrists.
exercises.hint: A quoted plural phrase as a single linguistic term takes a singular verb.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: is
A quoted plural phrase as a single linguistic term takes a singular verb.

exercises.question: Northern Lights ___ one of Suzanne's favourite books.
exercises.hint: Titles of books ending in -s take a singular verb.
exercises.explanation:
Answer: is
Titles of books ending in -s take a singular verb.
